Initial name-matching exercise found **14 plausible human first names**: **8 female · 3 male · 3 ambiguous/rare** Among the clearly gendered names: ::: {#047d0436 .cell fig-height='1.6' fig-width='5' execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/cell-2-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="53%"} ### And where did the names come from? **Ada** Named after **Ada Lovelace**, whose work on Babbage's Analytical Engine made her one of the foundational figures in programming. **Alice** Named after Lewis Carroll's ***Alice's Adventures in Wonderland*** — reflecting the idea of learning through exploring virtual worlds. **Julia** No historical Julia at all. Stefan Karpinski's explanation: > *“There's no good reason, really. > It just seemed like a pretty name.”* ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"} ### 👀 Coincidence? **Programming may be male-dominated, but programming languages with human first names seem decidedly female-dominated.** 😄 ::: Sources: Wikipedia, *List of programming languages*; Ada, Alice and Julia histories. ``` # Which of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals feels closest to your research? {.unnumbered} ## United Nation's Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) ```{=html}
``` ## United Nation's Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) :::: columns ::: {.column width="55%"} The SDGs constitute a framework for addressing the world's most pressing challenges. They provide a shared language and set of objectives for governments, organizations, and researchers to align their efforts toward a sustainable future [@un_2030_agenda_2015].
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false title="Definition of sustainable development"} As the departure point serves the **Brundtland report** issued by @wced_our_common_future_1987: > *Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.* ::: ::: ::: {.column width="5%"} ::: ::: {.column width="35%"} ![Brundtland report issued in 1987](./images/brundtland_report_book_cover.jpg){width=80%} ::: :::: ## SDGs get operational through quantifiable indicators :::: columns ::: {.column width="5%"} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} Sustainability becomes operational via indicators that bridge between SDG goals and tangible outcomes. **Indicators can be measured, predicted and optimized for with computational methods.** **Example: Indicator 7.2.1** - **2015:** 15.6% - **2023:** 18.0% ::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"} **Sources** : * UN SDG Report 2026 [@un_sdg_report_2026_goal7] * UN metadata for indicator 7.2.1 [@un_sdg_metadata_721]. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.sdg-taxonomy-card} ::: {.sdg-taxonomy-flow} ::: {.sdg-taxonomy-step} **Goal 7** Affordable and Clean Energy ::: ::: {.sdg-taxonomy-arrow} ↓ ::: ::: {.sdg-taxonomy-step} **Target 7.2** Increase the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix ::: ::: {.sdg-taxonomy-arrow} ↓ ::: ::: {.sdg-taxonomy-step} **Indicator 7.2.1** Renewable energy share in total final energy consumption ::: ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Computational Science and Engineering (CS\&E) ::: {.framework-card .cse-overlap-card}
... sits at the intersection of applied mathematics, computer science and applications in engineering and science.
:::: columns ::: {.column width="60%"} **Motivation:** Model-based design or ~ decision-support in complex systems of physics-based or mechanistic core. **Objective:** Uncertainty-aware and error-controlled prediction, introspection or reanalyis of coupled processes. **Focus:** Methods, algorithms, implementation, and software along with their effective deployment. **Challenges:** Given by multi-physics and multi-scale coupling, complex geometries, boundary conditions, the necessity for high-throughput tasks and data-rich workflows. ::: ::: {.column width="40%"}
![](./images/cse-overview.png) ::: :::: ::: ## How CS\&E enters the sustainable development goals ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} **Area 1: Optimizing energy systems** relevant to ::: {.sdg-icon-list} - ![SDG 7](sdg-icons/E-WEB-Goal-07.png){.sdg-bullet-icon} [**SDG 7:** Affordable and Clean Energy]{.sdg-bullet-label} - ![SDG 9](sdg-icons/E-WEB-Goal-09.png){.sdg-bullet-icon} [**SDG 9:** Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure]{.sdg-bullet-label} ::: ```{=html}

Left: Convection-coupled phase-change; Right: Mushy-layer evolution

``` ::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"} **Source**: *Stable across regimes: A mixed DG method for Darcy–Brinkman–Stokes type flows* [@terschanski2025stable] ::: ::: ::: {.column width="48%"} **Area 2: Geohazard prediction** relevant to ::: {.sdg-icon-list} - ![SDG 13](sdg-icons/E-WEB-Goal-13.png){.sdg-bullet-icon} [**SDG 13:** Climate Action]{.sdg-bullet-label} - ![SDG 11](sdg-icons/E-WEB-Goal-11.png){.sdg-bullet-icon} [**SDG 11:** Sustainable Cities and Communities]{.sdg-bullet-label} ::: ::: {.harmonized-figure-caption} ![Left: landslide database; right: data enrichment strategy.](./images/FAIR-susceptibility.jpeg){width="90%"} ::: ::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"} **Source**: *A modular framework for FAIR shallow landslide susceptibility mapping based on machine learning* [@edrich2024fairlandslides] ::: ::: :::: ## Sustainability and CS\&E **Observation**: CS\&E often contributes indirectly, but rarely names sustainability explicitly: ```{=html}

Application-facing view

  • sustainability is a societal objective
  • SDGs are visible in application-facing projects
↔

Method-oriented view

  • CS&E is an enabling technology
  • sustainability is rarely explicit in method-oriented CS&E research
``` CS\&E publications focus on accuracy, runtime, scalability, and robustness, yet rarely frame methodological design as sustainability choices. That mismatch motivates a second question. > > If CS&E helps design a more sustainable world, how sustainable is CS&E itself? > ## Sustainability from three pillars to sustainable CS\&E ```{=html}

Sustainability dimensions

Social
sustainability

Fair labor, human rights, and equitable access to resources.

Environmental
sustainability

Healthy ecosystems, conserved resources, and reduced environmental harm.

Economic
sustainability

Long-term viability, resilient value creation, and responsible resource use.

Sustainable CS&E dimensions

Sustainable computing

  • resource-aware models
  • efficient algorithms
  • energy-aware workflows

Sustainable software

  • reusable code
  • reproducible results
  • maintainable ecosystems

Stakeholder action

  • incentives
  • infrastructure
  • education

Sustainable CS&E emerges when these three dimensions reinforce each other.

``` ## Three sustainability aspects, and why they matter now ```{=html}

Three sustainability aspects within CS&E

  1. Energy footprint of computational work
  2. Longevity and reuse of CS&E knowledge
  3. Future relevance of CS&E in an AI-rich landscape

Why this matters now

  • workflows are becoming more complex
  • software stacks are becoming more fragile
  • AI-HPC pipelines increase both opportunity and waste
  • scientific value is easily lost in irreproducible computation
``` ## Part 2: Where sustainability began

``` ## The idea of sustainability based on Carlowitz We typically attribute the sustainability idea to **Hans Carl von Carlowitz**. - early forestry formulation in *Sylvicultura oeconomica* [@carlowitz_1713_biblio] - manage forests such that harvest does not outrun regrowth - it turned forest use into an explicit long-term management problem - ideas existed before Carlowitz, but he made them operational and widely known ::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"} > "..." > Daß es eine continuirliche, beständige und *nachhaltende Nutzung* gebe, weil es eine unentbehrliche Sache ist, ohne welche das Land in seinem Esse nicht bleiben mag. > --- *Hans Carl von Carlowitz, Sylvicultura oeconomica* [@carlowitz_1713_biblio] ::: ## Carlowitz' motivation was economic pressure ::: columns ::: {.column width="34%"} Carlowitz was a mining administrator in Saxony facing a **decision-support problem**: - reconstruction after war - expanding mining and metallurgy - rising timber prices and transport distance - growing pressure on economically accessible wood **His core question**: ::: ::: {.column width="66%"} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::::: How do we keep a resource-dependent system running when demand grows faster than renewal? ## It's a time-scale challenge Key challenge: The scope of the decision rested on a time-scale much shorter than the regeneration time of the system it controlled. *Sustainable forest management* requires predictive decision support whenever resource response times exceed operational decision horizons ```{=html} ``` ## From Carlowitz to the Sustainable Development Goals :::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.sdg-taxonomy-card} **Carlowitz**: One renewable resource, one stock, one regeneration process $$S_{t+1}=S_t+G_t-H_t$$ ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.sdg-taxonomy-card} **SDGs today**: Many interacting resources, many coupled indicators, many delayed responses 17 Goals  •  169 Targets  •  >230 Indicators ::: ::: :::: ```{=html}
A common principle:
When regeneration is slower than decision cycles, today's decisions determine tomorrow's possibilities. Sustainability is not mainly about indicators. It is about governing delayed dynamics: $$T_{\mathrm{system}} > T_{\mathrm{decision}}$$
``` ## Let's model and formalize ```{=html}

State and dynamics

Resource R(t)

Dynamics

$$ \frac{dR}{dt}=G(R)-D(R)+E $$

  • G: regeneration
  • D: depletion
  • E: managed intervention

Governance and viability

Decision u(t)

Implementation

$$ \tau_I \frac{dI}{dt}=c\,u-I $$

  • c: compliance
  • I: realized impact
  • R(t)\in \mathcal{K}: viable region
Sustainability means keeping a regenerating system inside a viable region despite delay, depletion, and imperfect implementation.
``` ## What changes from one domain to the next? ```{=html}

The structure stays the same

  1. resource
  2. regeneration
  3. depletion
  4. governance
  5. compliance
  6. viability

Only the interpretation changes

  • forest: timber stock
  • software: usability
  • methods: methodological capability
  • computing: effective compute
  • humans: scientific capability
``` ## Part 3: Where sustainable CS&E could go next

``` ## The internal perspective ```{=html}

If CS&E wants to be credible

  • it must reflect on its own energy footprint
  • it must preserve its software and knowledge
  • it must sustain its future methodological relevance

The three sustainability dimensions

  1. sustainable computing
  2. sustainable software and methods
  3. sustainable human capability
If CS&E helps design a more sustainable world, it must also sustain its own computational ecosystems.
``` ## CS\&E bottlenecks are shifting ::: columns ::: {.column width="48%"} **Traditional bottlenecks** - compute access - parallelization competence - memory and storage - raw implementation effort ::: ::: {.column width="52%"} **Emerging bottlenecks** - workflow complexity - software fragility - reproducibility gaps - AI integration - long-term maintainability ::: :::: ## Sustainable computing is about deliberate trade-offs It asks how computational work should be designed so that scientific benefit, runtime, and resource use are balanced consciously. ## Available compute is a finite regenerative resource ```{=html}

Resource

Available compute C(t)

Includes hardware, energy, queue time, cloud access, budget, and carbon budget.

$$ \dot C = G_C - L_C $$

Interpretation

  • GC: hardware, energy efficiency, funding, algorithms
  • LC: larger simulations, UQ, optimization, digital twins
  • finite computational opportunity must be allocated deliberately
The key question is not how to minimize compute at all costs, but how to turn finite compute into the most trustworthy insight.
``` ## Green computing versus sustainable computing ```{=html}

Green computing asks

How can we reduce computational energy consumption?

Important, but incomplete.

Sustainable computing asks

$$ K=\eta(M)\,C $$

  • K: generated knowledge
  • M: methodological capability
  • \eta = K/C: knowledge return per computational investment
The goal is not minimal compute. The goal is maximal trustworthy information return per computational investment.
``` ## Sustainable computing means allocating effort where it matters ```{=html}

Three levers

  1. Hardware efficiency
  2. Algorithmic efficiency
  3. Model efficiency

What that means in practice

  • invest degrees of freedom only where they matter
  • connect accuracy targets to computational effort
  • let quantities of interest drive computational investment
  • spend extra effort only where it changes the answer materially
Adaptive methods increase effective compute because they increase the value extracted from each computational unit.
``` ## Regeneration and depletion in computational ecosystems ```{=html}

Regeneration

  • more efficient hardware
  • improved energy infrastructure
  • better scheduling
  • adaptive numerical methods
  • improved software
  • AI-assisted workflows

Depletion

  • larger simulations
  • increasing model fidelity
  • uncertainty quantification
  • optimization and control
  • digital twins
  • more ambitious scientific questions
``` ## Monitoring resource consumption - measurement creates visibility - visibility enables accountability - accountability can shape better workflows ## Why ALUMET matters - application-level energy attribution is hard on shared CPU/GPU systems - runtime alone is often an unreliable proxy for energy consumption - sustainable CS\&E needs measurement that reflects actual computational cost - ALUMET helps close the gap between raw telemetry and actionable energy awareness ## ALUMET as enabler - modular, lightweight framework for energy and system measurement - plugin-based pipeline: gather, transform, export - adaptable across heterogeneous hardware and workflow contexts - enables downstream analysis and interpretation through tools such as Alumet-Insight - turns energy awareness into something usable for research software and workflows ## Software is the heart of CS\&E ```{=html}

Scientific role

  • software carries methods into practice
  • software preserves or loses knowledge
  • software quality shapes long-term scientific impact

The key shift

The sustained resource is not the artifact itself.

It is software usability inside an evolving ecosystem.

``` ## Sustainable software as a viability problem ```{=html}

Resource dynamics

Usability U(t)

$$ \dot U = -\delta U + \eta m $$

  • \delta: ecosystem drift
  • m: realized maintenance
  • \eta: maintenance effectiveness

Viability

$$ U(t)\ge U_{\min} $$

Software remains viable only if maintenance keeps pace with drift.

Software sustainability is an ecosystem problem: usability decays unless maintenance continuously regenerates it.
``` ## Planning versus implementation ```{=html}

Planned maintenance

Decision I(t)

What a group lead, PI, or project team intends to invest.

Realized maintenance

$$ m(t)=c(t)\,I(t) $$

Compliance determines how much planned work becomes actual upkeep.

``` ## Sustainable software means more than code availability ```{=html}

Properties of sustainable software

  • maintainability
  • reproducibility
  • accessibility
  • extensibility
  • portability
  • community uptake

Two failure modes

  • resource failure: too little maintenance planned
  • governance failure: maintenance planned, but not implemented
``` ## Sustainability emerges from feedback loops - usability increases adoption - adoption increases maintenance willingness - maintenance preserves usability - declining usability can trigger the opposite loop ## Sustainable methods as a race between questions and methods ```{=html}

Two evolving quantities

Required decision capability Q(t)

Available methodological capability M(t)

$$ \Gamma(t)=Q(t)-M(t), \qquad \Gamma \le 0 \text{ for viability} $$

Interpretation

  • demand drives innovation
  • success creates new demand
  • adaptivity slows obsolescence
  • continuous innovation is required just to keep pace
Computational science is a race between expanding questions and the community's ability to answer them.
``` ## Methodological success creates future demand - more methods enable more ambitious questions - more ambitious questions raise required decision capability - adaptivity slows methodological obsolescence - continuous innovation is required merely to keep pace ## Sustainable human capability ```{=html}

The regenerative layer beneath CS&E

  • education
  • mentoring
  • scientific collaboration
  • methodological training

The AI tension

  • AI can amplify short-term productivity
  • it can also weaken long-term learning loops
  • capability matters more than output spikes
  • researchers regenerate methods, software, and judgment
Human capability is the deepest regenerative resource in CS&E because it renews every other layer of the ecosystem.
``` ## Human capability regenerates the whole stack ```text Human capability ↓ Methodological capability ↓ Software usability ↓ Effective compute ↓ Decision capability ``` ## Sustainable CS\&E needs structure, not only goodwill ```{=html}

Why individual goodwill is not enough

  • sustainable practice often has delayed returns
  • short projects reward local optimization
  • institutions shape what is feasible and visible

Stakeholders who shape sustainable CS&E

  • funding agencies
  • supercomputing centers
  • research institutions
  • journals and publishers
  • industry and project leaders
  • educators and young scientists
Sustainable CS&E requires sustainable computing, sustainable software, sustainable human capability, and coordinated institutional support.
``` ## My stronger claim today The manuscript was necessary. Sustainable CS\&E is not merely a topic area. It is a methodology. ## The core methodological question Sustainable CS\&E asks: How do we maximize trustworthy information return per computational investment? ## Computational investment and information return ```{=html}

Computational investment includes

  • compute time
  • energy
  • human development effort
  • workflow complexity
  • software maintenance
  • data generation and curation

Information return includes

  • reduced uncertainty
  • trustworthy predictions
  • actionable design guidance
  • transferable method knowledge
  • reusable software and workflows
The methodological task is to increase trustworthy information return per unit of computational investment.
``` ## This is already native to CS\&E - error control already asks what accuracy is needed - adaptivity already allocates resources selectively - model hierarchies already trade cost against insight - numerical analysis already disciplines approximation ## Sustainable CS\&E is principled approximation The point is not to compute less at all costs. The point is to compute as much as needed, for the right reason, at the right fidelity. ## AI makes this more urgent - AI can amplify scientific productivity - AI can also amplify waste, opacity, and fragility - CS\&E has the tools to make AI workflows more principled ## My synthesis Sustainable CS\&E is the disciplined pursuit of lasting scientific value from computational effort. ## Final message If CS\&E wants to remain a key enabling discipline, it must make sustainability explicit in how it designs methods, software, and workflows. ## Thank you Questions and discussion
